  CONSIDERATION OF A CHARTER AMENDMENT MEASURE
  ESTABLISHING A SYSTEM OF POLICE OVERSIGHT (For the
  November 2020 General Election ballot, the last scheduled City
  Council meeting prior to the August 7, 2020 deadline to approve
  submittal of a Charter Amendment Measure occurs on August 3,
  2020)

  The two above agenda items were discussed concurrently

  Councilmember Kennedy, Chair of the Public Safety Committee
  (PSC), provided introductory comments, spoke on the
  correspondence received expressing various strong views on the
  creation of a Community Police Oversight Commission (CPOC)
  and an Independent Police Auditor; and responded to questions.
  Mayor Tomek presented a PowerPoint on a proposal for the
  creation of a CPOC; and responded to questions.

  Councilmember Madison expressed concerns that the creation of
  a CPOC may dilute the authority of elected representatives on the
  City Council and who also serve on the Public Safety Committee;
  and the CPOC may become a political body, with individuals
  serving on the appointed commission for political interests without
  direct accountability to voters and the community as a whole .
.....
  City Manager Mermell provided information on the appointment of
  a proposed auditor, and staff's use of external auditors; and
  responded to questions.

  Vice Mayor Hampton stated that he believes a model where the
  City Manager is responsible for hiring an independent auditor and
  as well as the Chief of Police is problematic in terms of
  independence. He noted the apparent conflict with one individual
  serving as both the City Attorney and City Prosecutor, and
  recommended that the City Council re-establish the Office of the
  City Prosecutor as a separate position.

  Councilmember Wilson thanked the Public Safety Committee
  (PSC) for their work on this item, and spoke on the need to
  continue to support Police Chief John Perez. He suggested that
  members of the PSC can serve on the CPOC in order to have
  elected individuals serve on the commission and also have direct
  accountability to the community.

  Javan Rad, Chief Assistant City Attorney, provided information on
  the "Pursuant to the Public Safety Officers Bill of Rights Act"
  (POBAR), which is provides procedural rights to Police Officers;
  and responded to questions.

  Council Minutes  9  07/27/2020
   Councilmember Gordo expressed concerns with the process and
  lack of transparency used to develop the proposed CPOC, which
  he believes was not drafted in concert with the public or the full
  Public Safety Committee. He also expressed concerns with all the
  information received related to policing, planning, development,
  response to COVID-19, and cannabis coming though the Office of
  the City Manager. He spoke in favor of an Inspector General to
  review the integrity of the City's processes and provide information
  to the City Council and public that is truly independent. He also
  spoke on his request to agendize a discussion on concerns related
  to "behested contributions" made to members of the Council,
  which was not agendized as requested. Councilmember Gordo
  spoke in favor of a police oversight model that includes the
  creation of an Office of Inspector General, hired through the City
  Prosecutor's Office or City Attorney's Office, including
  investigators, attorneys, and individuals that would report directly
  to the City Council, with a charge to review best practices and
  procedures in policing, development, and health. Councilmember
  Gordo asked the City Attorney to provide a clear understanding of
  the City Charter in this regard, and the rights and authority that
  currently exist for the City Council to exercise under the Charter,
  including subpoena power and ability to compel testimony for
  policing. He also requested a report on the City's subpoena
  authority and right to compel testimony through a proposed
  Inspector General position related to policing.

  Councilmember McAustin thanked the Public Safety Committee
  for their work on the proposed CPOC and spoke in favor of
  creating a community-based oversight body of the Police
  Department. She believes civilian oversight could provide input on
  how to demilitarize the police and that the Department should
  reflect the community; and is strongly opposed to a
  Councilmember or an elected official, being part of such a civilian
  police oversight board, nor should a Councilmember have
  authority to appoint a board member. She spoke in favor of
  requiring board members to complete 30 hours of training. She
  suggested that all interested community members that wish to
  serve on such a body should submit to 30 hours of training and
  then staff can conduct a lottery system for the final board
  members. In addition, she believes that the board members
  should be made up of 50% women.

  Councilmember Masuda asked staff to provide comparative
  demographics data and information on the Pasadena Police
  Department's leadership and those of the nation. He stated that
  he believes the Public Safety Committee and the City Council are
  elected by residents to provide oversight to the City Manager and
  the Police Department, and expressed concerns with a proposed
  CPOC made up of residents and others who may have their own
  agendas and could undermine a fair process.

Council Minutes  10  07/27/2020

  return to the Public Safety Committee to discuss the history of
  police oversight and for staff to provide an analysis on the City of
  Los Angeles, County of Los Angeles, and other local agency
  police oversight models.

  Vice Mayor Hampton presented information to the City Council to
  direct the City Attorney to prepare a Charter Amendment ballot
  measure to be voted on by Pasadena voters to establish and
  empower a Community Police Oversight Commission; and
  responded to questions. He spoke on the need for the City
  Council to receive an independent legal opinion on the issues
  related to the creation of an auditor position that reports to the City
  Council.

Council Minutes  14  07/27/2020
   Michele Beal Bagneris, City Attorney/City Prosecutor, stated that
  in addition to the fact that the creation of a potential auditor
  position is currently on the agenda, there are other legal and
  conflict interest issues that apply with respect to access to
  personnel records of Police Officers, which may have legal
  ramifications; and responded to questions.

  Councilmember Wilson stated that he shares the community
  concerns related to the independency of an auditor position in the
  City in terms of the hierarchy reporting relationship. He spoke on
  the work of the City's Internal Audit Manager, which he believes
  has merit, and is a viable strategy for police oversight in the City.

  Councilmember Kennedy stated that he believes that both the
  proposal for the creation of a Community Police Oversight
  Commission (CPOC) and an Independent Police Auditor may be
  an avenue to move forward, and modifications can be made at any
  time during the process and in the future as needed.

  Councilmember Gordo asked staff to provide information on how
  the City Council was able to authorize subpoena authority for the
  Code Enforcement Commission, and to determine such authority
  may be similarly applied to a proposed CPOC, with the
  understanding that any subpoena authority will be measured by
  the constitutional rights of individuals.

  Following discussion, the Mayor stated that staff needs to work
  with Vice Mayor Hampton to prepare City Charter language so that
  the City Council can consider the option of a Charter Amendment.

  CouncilmemberWilson stated that he is not in favor amending the
  City Charter for this purpose at this point, and would rather staff
  focus their work on evaluating a City Prosecutor model auditor,
  address other questions detailed above, and that the Public Safety
  Committee continue to discuss the proposed CPOC.

  Councilmember Madison expressed concerns with the notion that
  the City Council is working under a deadline, and does not believe
  the November 2020 ballot deadline is achievable. He noted that
  such a discussion, which he believes is a major policy initiative,
  should include additional outreach, thorough deliberation, and a
  Charter study taskforce on charter reform.

  Following discussion, on the order of the Mayor, and by
  consensus of the City Council, the item was continued to the next
  City Council meeting scheduled for Monday, August 3, 2020 for
  further discussion, with staff directed to return with the information
  as requested and detailed above.
